problemText: A map's legend shows a star inside a circle to mark capital cities, thin black lines to show borders between countries, and different flat colors filling in each country. What is the main job this map is built to do?
choices: Show the human-made boundaries and place names of countries and cities.
Display how high or low the land sits across different elevations.
Show how much rainfall falls in each part of the country during a year.
Illustrate which natural features such as rivers and mountains are located where.
hints: Look at what the legend actually lists: borders, a capital-city marker, and country colors.
Ask yourself: does the legend describe the shape of the land, data spread across an area, or human-made places and boundaries?

problemText: A geographer wants to study which areas of a region have the most people living in them. She creates a map where light tan means 'fewer than 10 people per square mile,' medium brown means '10 to 50 people per square mile,' and dark brown means 'more than 50 people per square mile.' What type of map has she made, and why does that map type fit her purpose?
choices: A political map, because different colors help separate one country from another country and the legend lists borders, capitals, and place names.
A thematic map, because it shows how one chosen kind of information — population spread — changes from place to place.
A physical map, because brown colors on a map always show elevation and the shape of the land using height and terrain symbols.
A climate map, because the map uses different shades of color to represent data values that vary across different geographic regions.
hints: The legend does not list borders or capitals, and it does not list elevation colors. Eliminate those two map types first.
What single topic does the legend track across the whole region? Is that the definition of a thematic map?

problemText: Two students are looking at the same country on a map. One student says, 'I can see green in the south and brown in the north, so the south must be flatter and the north must be mountains.' The legend, however, lists green for 'wheat-growing areas' and brown for 'dairy-farming areas.' Is the student's reasoning correct, and what type of map is this really?
choices: Yes, the student is correct, because green on a physical map always means low elevation and brown always means highland terrain.
No, the student made an error by assuming green always shows flatland and brown always shows mountains when used on physical maps showing elevation zones.
No, the student assumed the colors show elevation, but the legend lists what type of farming is done in each area instead. This is a thematic map.
No, because the student did not check the legend first to see what the brown and green colors were actually meant to represent on this particular map.
hints: Do not guess the map type from the colors alone. Read what the legend actually says the colors stand for.
Physical-map colors stand for elevation. What do these colors really stand for according to the legend?

problemText: A student looks at three different maps of the same country. The first legend lists elevation colors — green for low and brown for high — plus mountain-peak symbols. The second legend lists country borders, capital cities, and state borders. The third legend lists a single color scale showing temperature ranges from cool to hot across all regions. The student claims, 'The country looks completely different on each map because mapmakers are bad at their jobs.' Explain why the student's reasoning is wrong and why the maps actually look different.
choices: The maps look different because mapmakers use different colors and symbols arbitrarily without following any real rules or standards.
The maps look different because one is a physical map and two are political maps, so the physical map stands out visually.
The maps look different because the country's actual geography and borders changed between the time each map was made.

The maps look different because each map is built around a different legend to show a different kind of information — one shows natural landforms, one shows political boundaries, and one shows data about temperature. Each map type has a different job.
hints: Remember that every map is built around one main job. What is the job of each of the three legends described?
A political map, physical map, and thematic map of the same place would not look alike. Why not?

problemText: A teacher gives four students a blank map of a region and asks each student to create a map. Student A creates a legend listing which type of mineral is mined in each area. Student B creates a legend listing rivers, mountain peaks, and elevation colors. Student C creates a legend listing administrative region borders and capital cities. Student D creates a legend listing which language is most commonly spoken in each area. Which two students created thematic maps?
choices: Students A and B, because thematic maps use color and symbols more effectively to display information than other map types.
Students A and D, because each legend shows one chosen kind of information spread across different areas.
Students B and C, because physical maps and political maps are the most common types created in geography classes.
Students C and D, because these maps focus on human features such as cities, languages, and cultures rather than landforms.
hints: Identify what each legend is built to show. Does each one list a single chosen topic spread across the area, or does it list something else?

Student A's map shows mining areas — one type of data spread across a region. Student D's map shows languages — also one type of data spread across a region. What do these two have in common that the others don't?

problemText: Three maps of the same forest region exist. Map 1's legend shows elevation colors and river symbols. Map 2's legend shows 'protected wildlife areas' in green and 'areas open to logging' in yellow. Map 3's legend shows county borders, town names, and a capital marked with a star. A ranger asks, 'Which map should I use to find out where the mountains are?' A land-use planner asks, 'Which map shows me where forests can be cut down?' A government official asks, 'Where is the county boundary line between these two counties?' For each question, which map answers it best, and why does the other two not fit?
choices: Map 1 answers all three questions because it shows the most information at once, making it the most practical choice for all users regardless of what they need to know.

Map 1 answers the ranger's question (it shows natural landforms); Map 2 answers the planner's question (it shows one chosen data topic spread across the area); Map 3 answers the official's question (it shows human-made boundaries). Each map has a legend built for a different purpose.
Map 2 answers all three questions because it shows both the natural features and the human-made divisions needed to locate mountains, logging zones, and county lines.

Map 1 answers the ranger's question because it displays elevation; Map 2 answers both the planner's question and the official's question since it shows land-use data including conservation boundaries that align with county lines.
hints: For each question, decide which map's legend is built to answer it. What single piece of information does each person need — landforms, land use, or human-made boundaries?

Remember: a physical map shows elevation and natural features; a thematic map shows one chosen topic; a political map shows boundaries and place names. Match the job to the map type, then match the question to the job.

problemText: The Equator is an imaginary line that circles Earth. What is the purpose of the Equator on maps and globes?
choices: To mark the location of the North Pole and the South Pole
To separate the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere
To separate the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere
To divide Earth into continents and oceans
hints: The Equator runs east and west, not from pole to pole.
Think about which pair of hemispheres uses north and south in their names.

problemText: A town is located south of the Equator. Using the two-question method taught for finding hemispheres, which hemisphere is determined by this location alone?
choices: Only the Eastern Hemisphere, because south of the Equator means you have crossed into the eastern half
The Western Hemisphere only; you cannot know the north-south position without more information
Both the Southern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere, because all places south of the Equator are also west of the Prime Meridian
The Southern Hemisphere only; the town's position east or west of the Prime Meridian still needs to be checked
hints: The two questions are always asked in the same order: north-south first, then east-west.
Knowing a place is south of the Equator answers one question completely, but you still need to ask the other question about the Prime Meridian.

problemText: A hiker is trekking and crosses the Prime Meridian while walking east. Before crossing, the hiker was in the Western Hemisphere. After crossing, which hemisphere does the hiker enter?
choices: The Eastern Hemisphere
The Northern Hemisphere
The Southern Hemisphere
The same hemisphere, because crossing the Prime Meridian does not change your location
hints: The Prime Meridian is the line that separates the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere.
Crossing a line while walking in one direction puts you on the opposite side of that line.

problemText: An explorer makes this claim: 'North America is in the Northern Hemisphere, so it cannot be in the Western Hemisphere.' Identify what is wrong with this claim and correct it.
choices: The claim is wrong because it confuses the role of the Prime Meridian with the role of the Equator; the Prime Meridian divides east from west, not north from south, so North America can be north of the Equator and still west of the Prime Meridian
The claim is incomplete because it answers only the north-south question; North America is in both the Northern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere

The claim is wrong because a place must be in exactly one hemisphere; since North America is north of the Equator, it cannot also be positioned relative to the Prime Meridian in a way that puts it in the Western Hemisphere
The claim is incomplete because the explorer checked only the location relative to the Equator but did not check the location relative to the Prime Meridian to determine the east-west hemisphere
hints: Remember that the two questions must both be asked—one about the Equator and one about the Prime Meridian.
Every place on Earth is in two hemispheres, one from the north-south pair and one from the east-west pair.

problemText: Two continents are described: Continent X lies entirely north of the Equator and entirely east of the Prime Meridian. Continent Y has land both north and south of the Equator, but all of it is east of the Prime Meridian. Which statement correctly compares how many hemispheres each continent occupies?
choices: Continent X is in four hemispheres and Continent Y is in two hemispheres
Continent X is in two hemispheres and Continent Y is in two hemispheres
Continent X is in two hemispheres and Continent Y is in three hemispheres
Continent X is in three hemispheres and Continent Y is in four hemispheres
hints: For Continent X, check each line: is it on both sides of the Equator? Is it on both sides of the Prime Meridian?
For Continent Y, the Equator runs across it, so land exists on both sides of that line; the Prime Meridian does not divide it.

problemText: A captain records this ship's journey: 'We started west of the Prime Meridian and south of the Equator. We sailed north and crossed the Equator on Monday. We continued sailing north and west until Friday, when we crossed the Prime Meridian.' Use the two-question method to determine which two hemispheres the ship occupied after all crossings were complete. Then explain why the ship's final position is in exactly two hemispheres and not four.
choices: Northern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere; the ship crossed only one line (the Prime Meridian) in each direction, so it entered only two of the four hemisphere sections
All four hemispheres; the ship crossed both the Equator and the Prime Meridian, which means it passed through every hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere; the ship's starting position determines its ending hemispheres regardless of direction of travel
Northern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere; although the ship crossed two lines, each line separates only one pair of hemispheres, and the ship ended up on one side of each pair
hints: Apply the two-question method: After crossing the Equator while sailing north, is the ship north or south? After crossing the Prime Meridian while sailing west, is the ship east or west?

A place is in all four hemispheres only if it sits in all four sections created by the two lines—that happens only when a large area like a continent has the Equator running across it AND the Prime Meridian running across it. A single point cannot occupy all four.

problemText: You are looking at a paper map for the first time. Near the top of the map, printed in large letters, you see the words "Mountain Valley Nature Reserve." What part of the map is this, and what question does it answer?
choices: It is the scale bar, and it answers the question of how big distances really are.
It is the legend, and it answers the question of what the symbols on this map mean.
It is the compass rose, and it answers the question of which way is north.
It is the title, and it answers the question of what this map is showing.
hints: This printed text is located near the top of the map.
Words printed on a map that name the place or subject the map is about go by a specific name.

problemText: A student is reading the Riverside Park Map and wants to know what a small star symbol stands for. The map has a compass rose pointing north at the top, a title reading "Riverside Park Map" near the top, and a small box in the corner listing symbols and their meanings. Where should the student look to find out what the star symbol means?
choices: The legend, because it pairs symbols with what they stand for.
The compass rose, because it shows the direction from one symbol to another.
The title, because it names what the entire map shows.
The scale bar, because it measures distances between symbols on the map.
hints: Think about which part of a map is built to explain what symbols mean.
This part is sometimes called a key and usually sits inside a small box.

problemText: On the Pinewood Trail Map, a hiker sees a small straight bar printed near the bottom corner. The bar has a tick mark in the middle dividing it into two sections. The left end is labeled 0 and the right end is labeled 1 mile. The hiker wants to know roughly how far apart two campsites are on the real trail. Which part of the map answers this question?
choices: The title, which identifies the specific trail, region, or area that the map represents to the reader.
The scale bar, which connects distances on the map to real-world distances.
The legend, which explains the meaning of each symbol, color, and marking used throughout the map.
The compass rose, which indicates the cardinal directions and helps orient the map to geographic north.
hints: This part is printed as a bar with distance markings on it.
It is the only part of a map that connects a length on the page to a real distance in the world.

problemText: A student holds the Forest Lake Campground Map and sees that two cabins are marked by small square symbols. On the printed page, the cabin marked with a red square is directly to the right of the cabin marked with a blue square. The compass rose on the map shows an arrow labeled N pointing toward the top of the page. Based on this information, in which direction is the red cabin from the blue cabin in the real world?
choices: South, because the compass rose points north at the top of the page and the red square is to the right of the blue square.
North, because the red square is higher on the page than the blue square.
East, because the arrow labeled N points to the top of the page, so the right side of the page points east.
West, because the compass rose shows all four directions and west is the opposite of east.
hints: First, use the compass rose to determine what direction each side of the page represents.
Once you know that the top of the page is north, you can figure out which direction the right side represents.

problemText: A student looking at the Hillside Park Map needs to answer two questions. Question 1: "How far apart are the two parking areas?" Question 2: "What does the small triangle symbol on the map stand for?" For each question, which map part should the student use to find the answer?
choices: For question 1, use the legend; for question 2, use the scale bar.
For question 1, use the title; for question 2, use the compass rose.
For question 1, use the compass rose; for question 2, use the title.
For question 1, use the scale bar; for question 2, use the legend.
hints: Remember that each part of a map is built to answer exactly one type of question.
A 'how far apart' question needs a part that connects page distances to real distances; a 'what does this symbol mean' question needs a part that explains symbols.

problemText: A student is looking at two different maps side by side: the East Ridge Trail Map and the West Ridge Trail Map. On the East Ridge map, the compass rose shows the arrow labeled N pointing toward the top of the page. On the West Ridge map, the compass rose shows the arrow labeled N pointing toward the bottom of the page. On both maps, a lake symbol appears in the same position—directly above a stream symbol on the printed page. Based on the compass roses shown on each map, which statement correctly describes the real-world direction from the stream to the lake on each map?
choices: On the East Ridge map, the lake is north of the stream; on the West Ridge map, the lake is south of the stream because each map has its own compass rose showing a different direction for the top of the page.

On the East Ridge map, the lake is east of the stream; on the West Ridge map, the lake is west of the stream because rotating the compass rose changes which real-world direction corresponds to each side of the printed page.
On both maps, the lake is north of the stream in the real world because the compass rose direction is the same on every map and symbols maintain their actual geographic positions.

On the East Ridge map, the lake is above the stream; on the West Ridge map, the lake is below the stream because the visual page positions of the symbols determine their real-world directions regardless of what the compass roses indicate.
hints: Always check the compass rose printed on the specific map you are reading, not just the positions of symbols on the page.
Two maps can have the same symbols in the same page positions, but if their compass roses point different ways, the real-world directions will be different.

problemText: According to the seven-continent convention used in most United States geography classes, name the continent that sits at the far southern end of the globe, surrounded entirely by ocean with no land connection to any other continent.
choices: Australia
Antarctica
South America
Africa
hints: This continent is at the far southern end of the globe, the opposite end from the Arctic.
Think about which continents stand completely alone, surrounded on all sides by water.

problemText: The Indian Ocean has Africa along its western edge and Australia along its eastern edge. Using the two-question routine for describing locations, which of the following correctly identifies what lies along the Indian Ocean's northern edge?
choices: South America sits along the Indian Ocean's northern edge
The Arctic Ocean sits along the Indian Ocean's northern edge
Asia sits along the Indian Ocean's northern edge
Antarctica sits along the Indian Ocean's northern edge
hints: The Indian Ocean is in the Southern Hemisphere. Think about which continents are north of it.
Africa and Australia are on opposite sides of this ocean, so what large continent must sit above them?

problemText: Europe and Asia are counted as two separate continents, even though there is no ocean or sea between them and they sit on one continuous landmass. Which of the following best explains why geographers still count them as two continents?
choices: The landmass between Europe and Asia contains so much water that it functions as an ocean barrier between the two regions
Europe and Asia are separated by cultural and historical traditions that developed independently over time, making them distinct enough to count as separate continents
Every continent must have a unique neighbor that no other continent touches, which requires Europe and Asia to be divided into two separate continental regions
A convention is an agreed-upon way to divide something so people can talk about it clearly, even though it could reasonably have been divided a different way
hints: A convention is a way a group of people has agreed to do something.
Think about whether there is only one correct way to count continents, or whether different geographers could reasonably make different choices.

problemText: A student uses the two-question routine to describe South America's location by asking: what touches South America along its edges? The student finds that North America connects to it by a narrow strip of land to the north, the Atlantic Ocean lies to its east, and the Pacific Ocean lies to its west. The student concludes there is nothing to the south. Which of the following correctly explains what the student is missing?
choices: The student forgot to check that Antarctica lies to the south of South America, separated entirely by ocean
The student made an error because every continent must have exactly four neighbors
The student is correct—South America is the only continent without anything along its southern edge
The student forgot to mention that a sea, not an ocean, lies to the south
hints: When describing a location, you should check what touches a place along its edges—this includes other continents and oceans both.
Which continent sits at the far southern end of the globe? Could it border anything to the south of South America?

problemText: Two students describe the location of the Atlantic Ocean. Student A says: "The Atlantic Ocean has North America and South America on its western edge, and Europe and Africa on its eastern edge." Student B says: "The Atlantic Ocean has Europe and Africa on its western edge, and North America and South America on its eastern edge." One student has made a direction error. To check for this error, you can use a flip-check method: if a place is on one side of the ocean, that same ocean must appear on the opposite side when viewed from that place. Which student is wrong and why?
choices: Student A is wrong because North America and South America are not actually located on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean from each other
Student B is wrong because when you flip the statement, Europe cannot be on the western edge of the Atlantic and also have the Atlantic on its eastern edge at the same time
Student B is wrong because the Atlantic Ocean is larger on the eastern side than the western side, so the direction labels must be reversed to match the actual size of each region
Student A is wrong because Europe and Africa are on different continents, so they cannot both be neighbors of the same ocean's eastern edge
hints: Use the flip-check: if Europe is on one side of the Atlantic, Europe must see the Atlantic on the opposite side when viewed from Europe's perspective.
Think about which direction Europe actually faces when looking toward the Atlantic Ocean.

problemText: A geographer explains that Earth's continents and oceans are divided and named using the seven-continent and four-ocean convention. The geographer notes that some other geographers combine Europe and Asia into one continent (giving six continents) and that some name a fifth ocean, the Southern Ocean, circling Antarctica, instead of counting that water as parts of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans. A student asks: "If different geographers divide the world differently, how can I know which division is correct?" A convention is an agreed-upon way that a group has chosen to divide something so they can talk about it clearly. Based on this definition, which answer best addresses the student's question?
choices: The answer depends entirely on where you live, since each country teaches its own division in schools and that region's convention is considered correct only within its borders
The seven-continent division is the only correct one because it is used by most geographers in the United States and appears in the majority of American textbooks

There is no single correct answer because a convention is an agreed-upon way to divide something that could reasonably have been divided differently; the key is to know which convention your source is using, not to find the only true one
Both divisions must be equally accurate because geographers have equal authority, so you should memorize both equally well and use whichever feels right
hints: A convention is simply the way a group of people has agreed to divide something so they can talk about it clearly.
Think about whether a convention is the only possible way to do something, or whether it is one reasonable choice among other possible choices.
